facts.raw_span: A 56-year-old man
recurrent skin lesion on the dorsum of his right thumb
four-year history of a lesion at that site
partial amputation of the thumb was performed in December 2016
the lesion reappeared at the distal aspect of the thumb stump
no significant medical history
took no medications
1.8 × 1.3 cm well-circumscribed, firm, non-tender, indurated lesion
no palpable lymphadenopathy was noted
enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph node presumed to represent metastatic disease

concepts.why: The patient's history of a recurrent skin lesion on the thumb, with a previous partial amputation and subsequent reappearance, along with the presence of an enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph node, suggests metastatic squamous cell carcinoma.

The patient's history of a recurrent skin lesion on the thumb, with a previous partial amputation and subsequent reappearance, could be consistent with basal cell carcinoma, although the presence of an enlarged lymph node is less typical for this diagnosis.

The patient's history of a recurrent skin lesion on the thumb, with a previous partial amputation and subsequent reappearance, along with the presence of an enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph node, could suggest Merkel cell carcinoma, a highly aggressive skin cancer.

The patient's history of a recurrent skin lesion on the thumb, with a previous partial amputation and subsequent reappearance, along with the presence of an enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph node, could be consistent with melanoma, although the description of the lesion does not specifically suggest this diagnosis.

The patient's history of a recurrent skin lesion on the thumb, with a previous partial amputation and subsequent reappearance, could be consistent with dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, a rare skin cancer.
